svg.title: Sentinel node against systematic lymphadenectomy: what is done, traded and missed
svg.desc: Schematic comparing sentinel lymph node biopsy with systematic lymphadenectomy: what each route does, what is traded for what, and what the sentinel route misses. The figure carries no leg lymphoedema figure of any kind. The first section draws the two routes. Sentinel lymph node biopsy: a tracer is injected into the cervix to find the few nodes the tumour would reach first, only those nodes are removed and pathology examines them in more detail, with immunohistochemistry where needed; FIGO 2023 states that lymph node staging should be performed in intermediate-high and high-risk patients and that sentinel lymph node biopsy is an adequate alternative to systematic lymphadenectomy for staging purposes. Systematic lymphadenectomy: the pelvic nodes, sometimes with the para-aortic nodes, are removed as a group whether or not they look abnormal; in the Italian randomised trial the median number removed was 30 (interquartile range 22 to 42) against 0; and the FIGO 2025 report states that since the development of sentinel lymph node biopsy the indications for full surgical staging lymphadenectomy are scarce. The second section gives the reliability of the sentinel route from three prospective studies, each with its own denominator, all three using full lymphadenectomy as the reference. FIRES (Rossi 2017; 10 US centres including community hospitals, 18 surgeons, clinical stage 1, all histological types and grades, cervical ICG injection with robotic assistance, 385 enrolled and 340 completing the reference standard): at least one sentinel node mapped in 86 per cent (293 of 340); sensitivity 97.2 per cent (95 per cent CI 85.0 to 100), with 36 of 41 node-positive patients mapping successfully and the metastasis found in the sentinel node in 35 of those; negative predictive value 99.6 per cent (97.9 to 100); and the words of the authors themselves, that sentinel lymph node biopsy will not identify metastases in 3 per cent of patients with node-positive disease. SENTOR (Cusimano 2021; 3 Canadian centres, clinical stage 1 grade 2 endometrioid or high-grade endometrial cancer, 126 of 156 high-grade, ICG): detection rate per patient 97.4 per cent (93.6 to 99.3), 87.5 per cent per hemipelvis, bilateral 77.6 per cent (70.2 to 83.8); sensitivity 96 per cent (81 to 100), with 26 of 27 node-positive patients identified; false-negative rate 4 per cent (0 to 19) and negative predictive value 99 per cent (96 to 100); and in 7 of those 27 node-positive patients, 26 per cent, the metastasis lay outside the conventional pelvic dissection field or needed immunohistochemistry to be found. SENTI-ENDO (Ballester 2011; a prospective cohort across 9 French centres, FIGO stage I to II, dual cervical tracer of technetium plus patent blue with systematic pelvic lymphadenectomy, 133 enrolled and 125 evaluable): at least one sentinel node mapped in 111 of 125; sensitivity per hemipelvis 100 per cent (63 to 100) with negative predictive value 100 per cent (95 to 100); sensitivity per patient only 84 per cent (62 to 95) with negative predictive value 97 per cent (91 to 99); and all three false negatives were type 2, non-endometrioid, endometrial cancer. A panel in the same section states the miss rate precisely, with node-positive patients as the denominator: FIRES puts it at 3 per cent, in the words of the authors that sentinel lymph node biopsy will not identify metastases in 3 per cent of patients with node-positive disease, and the SENTOR false-negative rate is 4 per cent, 1 of 27. So the figure does not say that sentinel biopsy is as accurate as taking them all; the accurate sentence is that the miss rate in prospective studies is 3 to 4 per cent and that the false-negative risk is higher in non-endometrioid cancer. The third section gives the randomised comparison of tracers: the FILM trial injected both dyes into the same patient (clinical stage 1 cervical and uterine cancer, 180 randomised, 176 evaluable); in the per-protocol analysis of 163 patients and 485 nodes, indocyanine green found 471 nodes (97 per cent) and blue dye found 226 (47 per cent), a difference of 50 percentage points (95 per cent CI 39 to 62), p less than 0.0001, while the share of what was found that pathology confirmed as lymphatic tissue did not differ, p equal to 0.33. The fourth section puts the two randomised trials of full lymphadenectomy on one balance. What it gains: nodal metastasis was found in 13.3 per cent against 3.2 per cent, a difference of 10.1 percentage points (95 per cent CI 5.3 to 14.9), p less than 0.001; and the median number of nodes removed was 30 against 0. What it costs: 81 women against 34 had an early or late post-operative complication, p equal to 0.001, in the same trial of 514. What it does not buy is survival: in ASTEC (n=1,408, 85 centres in 4 countries) overall survival gave a hazard ratio of 1.16 (95 per cent CI 0.87 to 1.54, p equal to 0.31) with an absolute difference at 5 years of 1 percentage point (−4 to 6), and recurrence-free survival a hazard ratio of 1.35 (1.06 to 1.73, p equal to 0.017) pointing if anything towards not dissecting, with both becoming non-significant after adjustment for baseline and pathology at 1.04 (0.74 to 1.45) and 1.25 (0.93 to 1.66); and in Benedetti Panici (n=514) 5-year disease-free survival was 81.0 per cent against 81.7 per cent with a hazard ratio for a first event of 1.10 (0.70 to 1.71), p equal to 0.68, and 5-year overall survival 85.9 per cent against 90.0 per cent with a hazard ratio for death of 1.20 (0.70 to 2.07), p equal to 0.50. The ASTEC conclusion is quoted: pelvic lymphadenectomy cannot be recommended as a routine procedure for therapeutic purposes outside of clinical trials. A further panel states what these trials do not answer: radiotherapy in ASTEC was randomised independently of the nodal result, so the trial answers whether the dissection itself has a therapeutic effect rather than whether knowing the nodal status is useful; both trials recruited before the sentinel era; Benedetti Panici dissected the pelvis only with no para-aortic dissection and did not randomise post-operative treatment. The fifth section is what is traded, and it deliberately carries no numbers: swelling in the leg is genuinely less common after sentinel biopsy, and how much less depends on who measures and how, because the same group of women measured four different ways gives entirely different conclusions; an arrow points instead to the article on leg lymphoedema, how to prevent it and how to manage it. The sixth section keeps the minimally invasive comparison from the previous part of the article in the same frame: LACE (n=760, stage I endometrioid) gave 4.5-year disease-free survival of 81.6 per cent against 81.3 per cent, a difference of 0.3 percentage points (95 per cent CI −5.5 to 6.1), meeting its pre-specified equivalence margin; LAP2 (n=2,616) gave a 3-year recurrence rate of 11.4 per cent against 10.2 per cent and 5-year overall survival of 89.8 per cent in both arms, yet did not meet its own pre-specified non-inferiority threshold, hazard ratio 1.14 with a 90 per cent lower bound of 0.92 and a 95 per cent upper bound of 1.46; and the contrast is LACC in cervical cancer, where 4.5-year disease-free survival was 86.0 per cent with minimally invasive surgery against 96.5 per cent with open surgery — with the figure stating that LACC is a different cancer and a different operation, radical hysterectomy, and that the two must not be compared directly. The figure closes with three sentences it must not be read as. First, that sentinel biopsy is as accurate as taking them all — it is not, the miss rate in prospective studies is 3 to 4 per cent and higher in non-endometrioid cancer. Second, that nodes do not matter — they do, and what the two randomised trials show is that the dissection has no therapeutic effect, not that nodal status is unimportant. Third, that the reader should ask for one route or the other — the figure is a list of questions, and which route is used is decided by the gynaecological oncology team from histological type, grade and imaging.

g.text: SENTINEL NODE VERSUS FULL LYMPHADENECTOMY
Sentinel lymph node: what is
traded, and what is missed
On the left, a few nodes are taken; on the right, the whole
group. Each route brings its own denominators: detection
rate, sensitivity, false-negative rate, share of metastases
found, complications.
This figure carries no leg lymphoedema figure at all — that
number depends on who measures and how, and it has an
article of its own.
What each route actually does
Sentinel lymph node biopsy
A tracer is injected into the cervix to find the few nodes the
tumour would reach first.
Only those nodes are removed and sent to pathology, where they
are examined in more detail (with immunohistochemistry where
needed).
FIGO 2023: lymph node staging should be performed in
intermediate-high and high-risk patients, and sentinel lymph node
biopsy "is an adequate alternative to systematic lymphadenectomy
for staging purposes".
Systematic lymphadenectomy
The pelvic nodes, sometimes with the para-aortic nodes as well,
are removed as a group whether or not they look abnormal.
That is several times as many nodes — in the Italian randomised
trial the median was 30 (interquartile range 22 to 42) against 0.
The FIGO 2025 report: since the development of sentinel lymph
node biopsy, the indications for full surgical staging
lymphadenectomy "are scarce".
How reliable the sentinel route is: three
prospective studies, each with its own
denominator
All three used full lymphadenectomy as the reference, which is what
makes a false-negative rate calculable. In routine practice that
reference does not exist — which is the limit of what is known.
FIRES (Rossi 2017)
10 centres in the United States including community hospitals, 18 surgeons;
clinical stage 1, all histological types and grades; cervical ICG injection with
robotic assistance, followed by complete pelvic (and where indicated
para-aortic) lymphadenectomy. 385 enrolled, 340 completed the reference
standard.
At least one sentinel node mapped
Sensitivity
95% CI 85.0–100; of 41 node-positive patients, 36 mapped successfully and in 35 of
those the metastasis was found in the sentinel node
Negative predictive value
In the words of the authors themselves, sentinel lymph node biopsy
"will not identify metastases in 3% of patients with node-positive
disease".
SENTOR (Cusimano 2021)
3 centres in Canada; clinical stage 1 grade 2 endometrioid or high-grade
endometrial cancer (126 of 156 were high-grade); ICG; sentinel biopsy
followed by pelvic lymphadenectomy, with para-aortic dissection added for
high-grade disease. n=156.
Detection rate per patient
95% CI 93.6–99.3; 87.5% per hemipelvis; bilateral 77.6% (70.2–83.8)
Sensitivity
95% CI 81–100; 26 of 27 node-positive patients identified by the algorithm
False-negative rate
95% CI 0–19; negative predictive value 99% (96–100)
In 7 of the 27 node-positive patients (26%), the metastasis lay outside
the conventional pelvic dissection field or needed
immunohistochemistry to be found.
SENTI-ENDO (Ballester 2011)
A prospective cohort across 9 centres in France; FIGO stage I to II; dual
cervical tracer (technetium plus patent blue) together with systematic
pelvic lymphadenectomy. 133 enrolled, 125 evaluable.
At least one sentinel node mapped
Sensitivity per hemipelvis
95% CI 63–100; negative predictive value 100% (95–100)
Sensitivity per patient
95% CI 62–95; negative predictive value 97% (91–99)
All three false negatives were type 2 (non-endometrioid) endometrial
cancer — histological type affects how reliable this test is.
Saying "missed" precisely: the denominator is node-positive patients
FIRES puts it at 3%: in the words of the authors, sentinel lymph
node biopsy will not identify metastases in 3% of patients with
node-positive disease. The SENTOR false-negative rate is 4%, that
is 1 of 27 node-positive patients. So "sentinel biopsy is as accurate
as taking them all" is not what this figure says. The accurate
sentence is that the miss rate in prospective studies is 3% to 4%,
and that the false-negative risk is higher in non-endometrioid
cancer.
Tracer: this one was randomised within the
same patient
Indocyanine green
Blue dye
The FILM randomised trial injected both dyes into the same patient
(clinical stage 1 cervical and uterine cancer, 180 randomised, 176
evaluable). In the per-protocol analysis of 163 patients and 485 nodes,
indocyanine green found 471 (97%) and blue dye found 226 (47%), a
difference of 50 percentage points (95% CI 39–62), p<0.0001. The
share of what was found that pathology confirmed as lymphatic
tissue did not differ between them (p=0.33).
Full lymphadenectomy: two randomised
trials, put on one balance
What is gained, what is paid, and what is not bought — all three at
once.
What it gains
Share in whom nodal metastasis was found
a difference of 10.1 percentage points (95% CI 5.3–14.9), p<0.001; Benedetti Panici
Nodes removed (median)
30 vs 0
interquartile range 22–42, p<0.001
What it costs
Number of women with an early or late post-operative complication
p=0.001; the same trial, n=514
What it does not buy: survival
ASTEC (n=1,408, 85 centres in 4 countries), overall survival
hazard ratio 1.16
95% CI 0.87–1.54, p=0.31; absolute difference at 5 years 1 percentage point (−4 to
ASTEC, recurrence-free survival
hazard ratio 1.35
95% CI 1.06–1.73, p=0.017 — pointing, if anything, towards not dissecting; after
adjustment for baseline and pathology, overall survival 1.04 (0.74–1.45) and
recurrence-free survival 1.25 (0.93–1.66), neither significant
Benedetti Panici (n=514), 5-year disease-free survival
hazard ratio for a first event 1.10 (0.70–1.71), p=0.68
Benedetti Panici, 5-year overall survival
hazard ratio for death 1.20 (0.70–2.07), p=0.50
The ASTEC conclusion, in its own words: "Pelvic
lymphadenectomy cannot be recommended as routine procedure
for therapeutic purposes outside of clinical trials."
What these two trials answer is not whether nodal status matters
In ASTEC, post-operative radiotherapy was randomised
independently and had nothing to do with the nodal result — so the trial
answers whether the dissection itself has a therapeutic effect, not
whether knowing the nodal status is useful. Both trials recruited
before the sentinel era; Benedetti Panici dissected the pelvis only,
with no para-aortic dissection, and post-operative treatment was not
randomised. Reading them as "nodes need not be dealt with today"
goes well past what they show.
What is traded: this panel carries no numbers
Swelling in the leg: it is genuinely less common after sentinel
biopsy, and how much less depends on who measures and how —
the same group of women measured four different ways gives
entirely different conclusions, so this figure carries no
lymphoedema percentage at all.
the article on leg lymphoedema, how to prevent it and how
to manage it
The comparison from the previous section,
kept in the same frame
The two randomised trials of minimally invasive versus open
surgery in this cancer: LACE (n=760, stage I endometrioid) gave
4.5-year disease-free survival of 81.6% against 81.3%, a difference of
0.3 percentage points (95% CI −5.5 to 6.1), meeting its pre-specified
equivalence margin; LAP2 (n=2,616) gave a 3-year recurrence rate
of 11.4% against 10.2% and 5-year overall survival of 89.8% in both
arms, yet did not meet its own pre-specified non-inferiority threshold
(hazard ratio 1.14, 90% lower bound 0.92, 95% upper bound 1.46). The
contrast is LACC in cervical cancer: 4.5-year disease-free survival
of 86.0% with minimally invasive surgery against 96.5% with open
surgery.
LACC is a different cancer and a different operation (radical
hysterectomy). The two must not be compared directly.
Three sentences this figure must not be read as
First, "sentinel biopsy is as accurate as taking them all" — it is
not; the miss rate in prospective studies is 3% to 4%, and higher
in non-endometrioid cancer. Second, "nodes do not matter" —
they do; what the two randomised trials show is that the
dissection has no therapeutic effect, not that nodal status is
unimportant. Third, "so I should ask for one or the other" — this
figure is a list of questions; which route is used is decided by the
gynaecological oncology team from your histological type, grade
and imaging.
Schematic, redrawn from the FIGO 2023 staging paper, the FIGO 2025
report on cancer of the corpus uteri, FIRES (Rossi 2017), SENTOR
(Cusimano 2021), SENTI-ENDO (Ballester 2011), FILM (Frumovitz 2018),
the ASTEC surgical trial (2009), Benedetti Panici 2008, LAP2 (Walker 2009
and 2012), LACE (Janda 2017) and LACC (Ramirez 2018); the cohorts,
designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points
must not be compared directly.
